title: Design a payment gateway
summary: A model answer for a payment gateway that never charges a customer twice and can explain where every cent went.

topics.role: Makes a repeated payment call safe and keeps retries from adding load.
Explains why the ledger and the payment share one local transaction.
Limits retrying a provider that is likely to keep failing.
Covers the calls and the signed events a merchant depends on.
Shapes the keys and unique constraints the payment tables lean on.
Partitions payments and the ledger by merchant.
Frames the inbox and outbox tables and at-least-once delivery.

blocks.text: A payment gateway takes a merchant's request to charge a customer and carries it to the outside world that moves money: card networks, banks and the companies that connect to them. The gateway has no control over that world. It asks, waits, and has to cope when the answer is slow, late or missing. Nearly every hard part of this question comes from that one fact.
Questions to ask before drawing anything, each with the answer to say out loud if the interviewer lets you choose:

items: Who calls us? Merchant servers, through an API. A customer's browser never asks us to move money directly.
Do we see card numbers? No. The merchant's page sends card details to a separate vault and we receive a token that stands for them.
One step or two? Both. A merchant may charge in one go, or hold funds first and capture later.
How many outside providers? One at first, behind an adapter, so a second can be added without touching the rest.
What must never happen? A customer charged twice for one payment, and money that moved without a record of it.
What may be slow? Reports and old history. The path that starts and finishes a charge stays fast and available.

blocks.text: Scope in. Each item is here because it forces a real design decision:

items: Create a payment and ask the provider to authorize it.
Capture an authorized payment, in full.
Void an authorization that has not been captured.
Tell the merchant the outcome, in the reply and later by a signed event.
Keep an auditable record of every money movement and compare it with the provider's own reports.

blocks.text: Scope out. Each item is tagged as a feature or as a whole system that is its own interview question:

items: Card vault and tokenisation (whole system).
Fraud and risk scoring (whole system).
Paying merchants out to their banks (whole system).
Subscriptions, invoices and tax (whole system).
Refunds, partial capture and disputes (features; they reuse the same state machine and ledger, with new records going the other way).
Currency conversion (feature).

blocks.text: Leaving refunds out is safe because this design never edits history, so a refund is just a later, separate record. If the interviewer pulls refunds in, say that, and add them at the data model.
Tokenisation in one sentence: a token is a stand-in value for card details that live in a vault, and our systems store and pass only the token. The note below says why that matters for scope.

In its glossary, the PCI council defines the cardholder data environment as the components, people and processes that "store, process, or transmit cardholder data", which is why this design keeps card numbers out of the gateway.
Assumptions for the rest of this page: merchants call server to server, one region at first, one provider behind an adapter, card data kept out of our systems, and a token supplied by the client.

clarify.ask: We need a payment gateway for online merchants. Before you design anything, what would you ask me, and what would you leave out?
clarify.say: I would ask who calls us, whether we see card numbers, one step or two, and how many outside providers. Then I would say my scope back: merchants call from their servers, card details go to a separate vault and we only handle a stand-in value, and we start with one provider behind an adapter. In scope: create a payment, authorize it, capture it in full, void it, tell the merchant the outcome, and keep an auditable money record. Out of scope: the vault, fraud scoring, payouts, subscriptions, refunds and disputes. The thing that must never happen is a customer charged twice.
clarify.tip: Say the scope back in a few sentences, including what you leave out and why. A scope stated aloud is hard to change quietly later.

blocks.text: Functional requirements, kept short on purpose. A long list costs time you need for the hard parts.

items: A merchant can create a payment for an amount and currency against a payment-method token.
A payment can be authorized and captured later, or authorized and captured in one step.
A merchant can void an authorization that has not been captured.
A merchant learns the final outcome of every payment, by reply and by signed event.
Every movement of money is recorded in a ledger that can be audited and compared with provider reports.

blocks.text: Non-functional requirements, in rank order. The order is your answer to what gives way when two of them collide.

items: Correctness of money. One payment moves money at most once, and every movement that does happen is recorded. It ranks first because a slow system can be made faster later, while a wrong charge has already reached a customer.
Auditability. Any balance can be rebuilt from entries that are never edited or deleted.

Availability of the charge path. Merchants can start and finish payments while a provider is slow or a reporting job is behind. When we cannot tell what happened, the answer is pending and we do not guess.
Latency. The provider call dominates, so our own work stays small. We accept one extra write before the call to buy safety.
Scale. Write-heavy, with bursts around sales events and a few merchants far larger than the rest.

blocks.text: Look at the tension between the first and third items. Staying available while unsure means we need a third answer besides success and failure: pending. Much of the design exists to make pending safe and short-lived.
Estimation waits until a choice depends on it. Two numbers do, so they are stated as assumptions and then used.

Assume a large gateway with 500 payments per second on average and 2,000 at the peak, with about 4 ledger rows written per captured payment at about 200 bytes each. A smaller gateway can scale every figure down; the method stays the same.

Arithmetic from that assumption: 500 payments per second is about 43 million payments a day, so about 170 million ledger rows and about 35 GB a day, or about 13 TB a year. At the peak, 2,000 payments per second times 4 rows is about 8,000 ledger rows per second.

What the numbers change. This peak write rate looks plausible for one well-run relational primary per partition, so no exotic store is assumed. That holds only with synchronous commit switched on, which the failure modes section requires for the payment store because waiting for a replica lowers write throughput. A load test with it on settles the question. Storage growth never stops, so data is partitioned by merchant from day one and old rows move to cheaper storage on a schedule. Assume status reads stay modest next to writes; if they do not, a read replica or a cache is the first thing to add.

requirements.ask: What must the system do, which qualities matter most, and how big is it? Rank them and tell me which you would give up first.
requirements.say: Functionally: create a payment, authorize and capture it, void it, and tell the merchant the outcome by reply and by signed event, with every money movement recorded. In ranked order the qualities are correctness of money, auditability, availability of the charge path, then latency, then scale. Under the assumptions below the peak write rate looks manageable for one primary per partition, so storage growth and hot merchants matter more than raw throughput. I would give up scale headroom, then latency, before any of the first three. When we cannot tell what happened, the answer is pending and we keep the evidence.
requirements.tip: Rank the qualities and say what gives way when two collide. Do arithmetic only when the result changes a decision, and label every number as an assumption.

blocks.text: The nouns, as a first draft that the later sections refine:

items: Merchant: the business that owns payments, a webhook address and a signing secret.
Payment: the merchant's intent to collect an amount. It holds the amount, currency, the merchant's own order reference and the current state. This is what the merchant asks about.
Attempt: one try to move the money through a provider. It holds our reference for the provider, the time sent and the result: sent, approved, declined or unknown.
Money movement: one capture, void or refund request against a payment, with its own id, committed before the provider call it triggers. A ledger transaction is built from it.
Ledger transaction and ledger entries: the immutable money record. A transaction groups the entries that must balance.
Idempotency record: the saved answer to a request, kept under the key the client chose.
Inbound event: a notification from the provider, stored before anything acts on it.
Outbound event: a notification for a merchant, waiting to be delivered.

blocks.text: Payment and Attempt are split on purpose. A payment can need several attempts, for example a second provider tried after the first definitely rejected the request before processing. An unknown outcome keeps the same attempt. A decline of the card ends the payment as failed, and the merchant starts a new payment. The unknown outcome after a timeout belongs to the attempt. The payment itself moves only when a fact is known. Authorize uses an attempt, while capture, void and refund use a money movement, because an authorization holds funds and moves none, and the other three change what is held or owed and feed the ledger.

items: Created to authorized: the provider approved and holds the funds.
Created to failed: the provider declined, or the request was rejected for good. Failed stays final for the payment, but see the late-authorization rule below.
Authorized to captured: the merchant claimed the held funds.
Authorized to voided: the merchant released the hold.
Authorized to expired: the hold lapsed before anyone captured it.
One-step charges run created, authorized, captured back to back.

blocks.text: Captured, voided, expired and failed are final. A request for any other move is refused with a conflict. Later money events, such as a refund, are separate records that point at the payment, so its own state never travels backwards. Final states are what make a repeated or late message harmless, which the webhook dive uses. The one exception, a late authorization on a failed payment, is the next paragraph: failed is final for the payment, but money may still be held.

Pending is no payment state, and nothing stores it as one. The API gives it as the reply while a payment is created or authorized and an attempt or money movement for it is unresolved, meaning the provider has not answered or the answer is not yet known. The payment keeps its last known state until a fact arrives from recovery, an event or reconciliation. A merchant that sees pending keeps the order open, does not charge again and does not mark it failed; it waits for the signed event or asks with Get payment.

One late message needs a rule of its own. A bank can answer slowly, so the provider may authorize a payment after we already marked it failed. Do not drop that event and do not revive the payment. Record it, look the attempt up with the provider, and if the provider holds funds we do not mean to keep, void the hold automatically (or refund, if the money was taken) and log it as an exception for review.

Between them, Razorpay, Stripe and Adyen document slow bank answers, retries after a failure and authorization windows, so the state machine here is our own design; Adyen puts the window point briefly: "The length of an authorization's validity depends on the card scheme."

entities.ask: What are the main things the system stores, and what states can a payment be in? Draw the legal moves between them.
entities.say: The nouns are merchant, payment, attempt, money movement, ledger transaction and entries, idempotency record, and inbound and outbound events. A payment is the merchant's intent. An attempt is one try through a provider, so the unknown outcome after a timeout lives on the attempt. Payment states are created, authorized, captured, failed, voided and expired. Created goes to authorized or failed, and authorized goes to captured, voided or expired. The last four are final, so repeated or late messages cannot move a payment backwards. Pending is not a state: it is the reply while an attempt or movement is unresolved.
entities.tip: Split things when they change at different times or can repeat, such as an attempt and its payment. Draw the state machine, name the final states, and keep a derived answer like pending out of it.

blocks.text: Four calls for merchants, one signed event stream out, and one endpoint in for the provider. The caller's identity comes from its credential and the server sets all timestamps.

Merchant authentication. Each merchant holds a secret API key, sent on every call over an encrypted connection. We store only a hash of it, scope it (test or live, and which calls it may make), and let a merchant create a new key and retire the old one after an overlap. The key tells us who is calling, so a merchant id in a request body is never trusted.
Stripe's API keys guide describes rotating a secret key, which is the model for letting a merchant replace a key without downtime.

items: Create payment. Body: merchant order reference, amount as a whole number of the smallest currency unit, currency code, payment-method token, and capture mode (automatic or manual). Header: an idempotency key. Reply: payment id, state, and a pending flag if we have no final answer yet.
Get payment. By id. Reply: state, amounts, and a short list of attempts with their results.
Capture payment. By id, for the full authorized amount, plus an idempotency key.
Void payment. By id, plus an idempotency key.
Outbound event. We post to the merchant's address: event id, type, payment id, new state, created time.
Inbound event. The provider posts to our receiver; the same checks apply in reverse.

blocks.text: Stripe's currency guide sets the convention our whole-number amount follows: "All API requests expect amount values in the currency’s minor unit".
Status codes follow the usual classes, and the exact choice for each case is ours.

blocks.caption: Which HTTP status each case gets
rows: We have an answer
Success class
The reply holds the final state.
The reply is pending
Accepted
The work continues after the reply.
The body is bad
Client error (bad request)
Nothing was written.
A second copy arrives while the first still runs, or a retry finds a record left in progress
Conflict, with a retry-later hint
The first copy owns the key until it finishes.
A move is illegal from the current state, or a capture with a new key finds an earlier capture still open
Conflict
Our own choice; a payment has at most one open capture movement.
A key is reused with a different body
Unprocessable content
Almost certainly a client bug.
The merchant is over its limit
Too many requests
Protects the shared workers.

blocks.text: The IETF idempotency-key draft names the conflict for a request still running and the unprocessable-content status for a changed body, the two cases on this page that it supports.

The idempotency key is how a merchant safely repeats a call after a timeout. The client makes it, one per logical operation, and reuses it on every retry of that operation. The server saves a fingerprint of the request with the key. The same key with the same body returns the saved reply. The same key with a different body is an error, because it is almost certainly a bug. A second copy that arrives while the first is still running is answered with a conflict status that tells the client to retry later, and so is a retry that finds a key record a crashed process left in progress, until recovery finishes it. An in-progress record is kept until its attempt or movement is resolved. Once a record has expired, a retried create runs as a new request, and only the unique order reference stops a second charge; a retried capture is refused because the payment's final state refuses a second capture.

Adyen, Square and Stripe each document what a repeated request under one key receives, Square and Stripe also cover a changed request, and Adyen describes the replay case this way: "the response to the first attempt will be returned without duplication".

Async results. The create call waits for the provider only up to a deadline we set. If the deadline passes we reply pending, and the merchant learns the rest from a signed event or by calling Get payment. Polling works as a fallback, but events are cheaper for both sides.
Signing and verifying an event, the same on both directions of the exchange:

items: Sign the exact bytes of the body, with a secret shared with the receiver, and send a timestamp that is part of what is signed.
The receiver checks the signature on the raw bytes before parsing them, because parsing and re-encoding can change the bytes.
The receiver rejects a timestamp that is too old, so a captured request cannot be replayed later.
The receiver compares signatures in constant time.
The receiver saves the event id, ignores one it has seen, replies with a success status quickly and does the work afterwards.

blocks.text: Razorpay's webhook validation page shows the signature travelling in a request header, which supports signing the body with a secret shared with the receiver: "This hash signature is passed with each request under the X-Razorpay-Signature header that you need to validate at your end."
The Python hmac documentation addresses how to compare a received signature: "it is recommended to use the compare_digest() function instead of the == operator".

api.ask: Walk me through the calls a merchant makes, what each request and response holds, and how a merchant learns the result of a slow payment.
api.say: There are four merchant calls: create payment, get payment, capture and void. Each is authenticated by a secret key, and each write carries an idempotency key. Create takes an order reference, an amount in the smallest currency unit, a currency, a token and a capture mode. If the provider has not answered by our deadline we reply pending, and the merchant hears the rest through a signed event or by getting the payment. Events carry an id, a type, the payment id and the new state, signed over the raw body with a timestamp. A repeat of the same key returns the saved reply. Pending is a reply, not a state: the merchant keeps the order open and waits for the event or gets the payment.
api.tip: Derive the caller from its credential, let the server set timestamps, and say which calls are safe to repeat. Say that the first version will change, because the contract matters more than field names.

blocks.caption: Core records and why they are shaped this way
rows: Payment
id, merchant id, merchant order reference, amount, currency, state, version, times

Unique on merchant id plus order reference among payments that are not failed, voided or expired, so an order whose funds were released can be charged again as a new payment. The version number lets a state change succeed only if nobody moved the state first.
Attempt
id, payment id, provider reference, state, sent time, answered time
Written before the provider call. Its id is the reference the provider sees.
Money movement
id, payment id, kind (capture, void, refund), amount, state (sent, done, failed, unknown), idempotency key, time

Written before the provider call it triggers, in the same local transaction as the key record. Its id is the provider's idempotency key for that call. Several refunds on one payment each get their own row.
Ledger transaction
id, movement id, kind (capture, fee, reversal), time
The id is built from the movement id and the kind, and is unique, so posting the same movement and kind twice is refused.
Ledger entry
id, transaction id, account id, direction, amount, time
Insert only. The entries of one transaction add up to zero across accounts.
Ledger account
id, owner, type (provider receivable, merchant payable, fee income)
A balance is a checkpoint plus the entries since it; no balance field is updated.
Idempotency record
merchant id, key, request fingerprint, status, saved reply, expiry

Unique on merchant id plus key. Written in the same local transaction as the payment and its first attempt, or as a capture's or void's movement row. A record stays in progress until its attempt or movement is resolved, whatever the expiry.
Inbound event
provider event id, raw body, received time, processed time
Unique on provider event id. The body is stored before any logic runs.
Outbox event
id, payment id, type, body, attempts, delivered time
Written in the same transaction as the state change it describes.

blocks.text: Shared accounts such as provider receivable and fee income are held as per-merchant sub-accounts. A capture then touches only rows in the merchant's own partition and stays one local transaction. Company-wide totals are sums across those sub-accounts.

Indexes follow the questions we ask. Payments by merchant and id, and by merchant and order reference. Attempts by payment. Attempts and money movements by state and sent time, for the recovery worker to find stuck ones. Ledger entries by account and time, for statements and balances. Outbox rows by delivered time, for the relay to find undelivered ones.

Why the ledger is append-only. Money records are evidence. If a row can be edited, a bug or an attacker can change history and nobody can show it. If rows are only added, a mistake is fixed by adding a reversing entry, the history stays whole, and every balance can be rebuilt by adding up entries. It also removes a class of races, because inserts do not fight over one row.

Why double-entry. Every transaction moves an amount out of one account and into another, so its entries add up to zero. A lost or invented cent then shows as a transaction that does not balance, which a simple check can find. A ledger with single-sided entries has no such check.

In its 2019 post on its books service, Square describes an immutable double-entry ledger, and TigerBeetle's data-modelling guide describes the same shape; Square says it works "so each cent lost is matched with a cent gained".

DynamoDB's optimistic-locking guide describes version-number checks, the same idea as our check on a payment's state: updates "succeed only if the client-side object version matches the corresponding version number".

Where the idempotency record lives. In the same database as the payment, written in one local transaction with the payment and its first attempt. If they lived apart, a crash between the writes could leave a payment with no key or a key with no payment, and the key would stop protecting anyone. In one transaction, a crash cannot leave a key marked in progress with no attempt for recovery to find.
Assume idempotency records are kept for 72 hours.

Why retention needs a stated choice. The record must outlive the longest time a merchant's client keeps retrying, with margin, or a late retry is treated as new. Longer costs only one small row per request, so the limit is set by how long merchants retry. After the record expires, the unique order reference is the second line of defence: a second payment for the same order is refused while an earlier payment for that order is not failed, voided or expired. Keys and order references protect against different mistakes, so keep both.
Stripe and Adyen each state how long they keep an idempotency key, and the two periods differ, so ours is a choice.

data-model.ask: How do you store this? Show me the records, their key fields, what you index, and why the ledger looks the way it does.
data-model.say: Payments, attempts and money movements sit with the ledger transactions and entries in one database, partitioned by merchant. The ledger is insert only and double entry: each transaction's entries add up to zero, and a mistake is fixed by a reversing entry. Balances are sums of entries plus checkpoints. The idempotency record is written in the same transaction as the payment, unique per merchant and key, and kept for the window in the assumption below. A unique order reference covers the time after that. Inbound events are unique by the provider's event id.
data-model.tip: Tie every index to a query you can name, and say what each unique constraint protects against. Explain why a record is shaped as it is as well as what its fields are.

blocks.text: Start with the happy path in words, then build it one need at a time. After each step the drawing is a working system, and the last line of each step names what is still weak. The weak spots become the deep dives.
The happy path for a two-step payment:

items: Create: the merchant sends the amount, currency, token and an idempotency key. In one local transaction we store the key record, a payment in the created state and an attempt in the sent state.
Authorize: the adapter asks the provider, passing our attempt reference. The provider approves and holds the funds. We save the answer and move the payment to authorized.

Capture: later, the merchant asks us to capture. In one local transaction we commit the key record and a money-movement row in the sent state. We then ask the provider to take the held funds, using the movement id as its idempotency key. In a second transaction we save the answer, move the payment to captured and post balanced ledger entries.
Event: a signed event reaches the merchant through the outbox, and the provider's own confirmation, when it arrives, is matched against the payment.

blocks.text: Read the whole picture as three loops. The merchant loop is request, payment store, reply. The provider loop is adapter, provider, and the inbox for what the provider says later. The repair loop is the workers, which retry, ask the provider about stuck attempts and movements, send events and compare our records with the provider's reports.

stages.need: A merchant asks to charge a customer and gets an answer.
stages.add: A gateway API checks the request, writes a payment in the created state, calls the provider through an adapter, writes the result and replies.
stages.weak: A merchant that times out and retries makes a second charge. A crash after the provider answers loses the answer.

high-level.ask: Walk me through the first version of the system, and tell me where it is weak.
high-level.say: First a gateway API, a payment store and an adapter that calls the provider. That breaks when a merchant retries, so I add an idempotency key written with the payment. That leaves our own provider call unsafe, so I write an attempt row before the call. Next, a money-movement row committed before the capture call, with ledger entries in the same transaction as its result. Then an inbox for provider events and an outbox for merchant events. Last, a recovery worker for stuck attempts and movements and a reconciler that compares our ledger with the provider's reports.
high-level.tip: Keep the first drawing small enough to finish, make it work end to end, then grow it one need at a time. After each addition, say aloud what it still leaves open.

dives.title: The crash between the provider charging and us recording it
dives.attempt: Call the provider, wait for the answer, then write the result to our database.
dives.breaks: If the process dies after the provider takes the money and before our write, the card is charged and our record says the payment is only created. The merchant retries. We have no memory of a call, so we call again, and the customer is charged twice. The same hole opens when the provider is slow and our request times out.
dives.better: Write down the intention before acting. In one short transaction, commit the key record, the payment and an attempt row in the sent state with a reference we generated, then call the provider and pass that reference as its own deduplication key. Never hold a database transaction open across the call. Afterwards, save the answer and move the payment in a second short transaction. Capture and void follow the same rule with a money-movement row whose id is the provider's idempotency key. A recovery worker scans attempts and movements that have sat in sent longer than the call deadline plus margin and looks each up by reference. A found result goes through the normal path. A lookup that finds nothing proves nothing, since the request may be in flight or the lookup may lag, so the worker repeats the call with the same reference, which is safe whichever way the first call went while the provider still holds the key. Past the provider's retention window it resolves the attempt by lookup or reconciliation instead. Meanwhile the merchant's retry gets the retry-later conflict status until recovery finishes, as the API section describes.
dives.tradeoff: We pay one extra committed write before every provider call, and the merchant sees pending for the recovery delay after a crash. The design needs a provider that accepts our reference as an idempotency key or lets us look the request up. If a provider offers neither, the payment stays pending until its settlement report resolves it, and that gap should be said aloud.

real.text: Stripe's error-handling page deals with unclear outcomes after a connection failure and advises: "Retrieve the relevant object from Stripe and check its status."

dives.title: Duplicate and out-of-order webhooks
dives.attempt: When an event arrives, set the payment to the state it names and post any ledger entries it implies.
dives.breaks: Providers retry deliveries when a reply is late, so the same event can arrive more than once, and a second capture event would post the money twice. Events can also arrive in a different order than they happened, so a late authorized event can land after captured and drag the payment backwards. Doing the work before replying also makes the provider retry while we are still busy.
dives.better: Four rules. First, store the raw event in the inbound table under its provider event id, with a unique constraint, then reply with success straight away and process afterwards. A duplicate insert is ignored. Second, treat an event as a claim about a state and run it through the state machine. A move that is legal from the current state is applied. A move that would go backwards or sideways is recorded and dropped, with one exception: an event showing that the provider holds or took money for a payment we consider dead, such as a late authorization on a failed payment, goes to lookup and an automatic void or refund, logged as an exception. Third, when an event implies a state we have not seen yet, or the order is in doubt, ask the provider for the current state by reference and apply that. Fourth, give each ledger transaction an id built from the movement id and the kind, with a unique constraint, so even a bug cannot post one movement twice while several refunds on one payment, if refunds are added, still each post once.
dives.tradeoff: An extra read call to the provider for the unclear cases, an inbox table that grows and needs trimming, and a small delay between the event arriving and the payment moving. In return, delivery order and repeats stop mattering. Relying on provider timestamps for order is cheaper but trusts their clocks and their stated ordering rules.

real.text: Stripe, Adyen and Razorpay document repeated, late and reordered events, which supports storing, acknowledging first and deduplicating; Stripe says of order: "Stripe doesn’t guarantee the delivery of events in the order that they’re generated."

dives.title: Timeouts on the card network or bank: retry, or ask what happened?
dives.attempt: Set a timeout. When it fires, mark the attempt failed and tell the merchant to try again.
dives.breaks: After a timeout the charge may or may not have gone through, so a payment marked failed can be a charged card, and the merchant's retry creates a second charge. Retrying blindly at every layer also multiplies load on a provider that is already struggling.
dives.better: Sort every outcome into three kinds. A definite no, such as a decline or a rejection before processing, ends the attempt and can move the payment to failed. A definite yes moves it forward. Everything else is unknown: a timeout after the request was sent, a dropped connection, a server error with no usable body. An unknown outcome keeps the same attempt and the same provider reference. Then choose between retrying and asking. If the provider honours repeats under the same reference, retry the same request a small bounded number of times, with backoff and jitter, spending from a shared retry budget so a bad hour cannot turn into a flood. If the budget runs out, or the provider has no safe repeat, stop sending and ask: look up the reference, then wait for the event, then wait for reconciliation. Only one layer retries, and the total of timeouts and retries must fit inside the deadline we gave the merchant, or the merchant retries over the top of ours. Never move a payment with an unknown attempt to a second provider until the first has answered, or both may charge.
dives.tradeoff: More payments end as pending for a while, and merchants must handle that answer. Tight budgets keep a provider outage from spreading, and cost some payments that a longer retry would have saved. Choosing the timeout from the provider's observed latency tail trades the odd needless timeout for speed.

real.text: Amazon's 2019 post on timeouts and retries and Google's SRE chapter on cascading failures both treat bounded retries, and Amazon says: "A timeout or failure doesn't necessarily mean that side effects haven't happened."

dives.title: Keeping the ledger and the payment record consistent without a distributed transaction
dives.attempt: Run the payment service and the ledger service separately. Update the payment, then call the ledger, and wrap both in a two-phase commit so they succeed together.
dives.breaks: Two-phase commit makes every participant wait on a coordinator. If the ledger participant is down before it votes, the coordinator aborts, so no capture can complete while the ledger is out. The worse case is a coordinator that fails after participants have voted yes: they hold their locks and wait for it, which stalls captures. The provider cannot join the protocol at all, so it protects only part of the flow. Calling both in turn instead leaves a window where the payment says captured and the ledger has no entry, or the reverse.
dives.better: Start by shrinking the problem so that most of it needs no coordination. Keep the payment, its attempts, its money movements and its ledger entries in the same database, partitioned by merchant, so recording a capture's result is one local transaction: the state change, the balanced entries and the outbox row commit together or none of them do, after the movement row was committed before the provider call. Ids built from the movement id and the kind make a replay harmless. For anything that must reach another system, such as the merchant's event or an analytics feed, the outbox row is the promise: a relay reads committed rows and publishes them at least once, and the receiver deduplicates by event id. Where a flow truly crosses services, break it into local steps, each safe to repeat, and fix a failed step with a compensating entry that reverses it. A compensation adds a record and deletes nothing, so the money history stays whole.
dives.tradeoff: The payment and the ledger now scale together by merchant partition, so they cannot be split into independent services without paying coordination costs again. A transfer between two merchants on different partitions needs two local transactions and a relay between them. Consumers must be idempotent, and there is a delay between commit and delivery. In exchange there is no coordinator to block on.

real.text: The microservices.io outbox page describes publishing events from a committed change, the pattern behind this dive's outbox step: "Messages are guaranteed to be sent if and only if the database transaction commits".

notes: Scaling and the partition key. Partition by merchant id, hashed, so a payment, its attempts, its money movements and its ledger entries sit together and a capture stays a local transaction. Idempotency records, inbound events and outbox rows use the same key. Status reads go to the same partition by payment id, which carries the merchant id in it.

Hot merchants. One very large merchant first stresses single rows, so update no balance row per payment: balances are sums of entries plus checkpoints, and the key insert and the payment row, whose order reference is unique, go in one local transaction. Splitting a merchant's rows across sub-partitions inside one database relieves hot rows only. If the merchant saturates the primary, give it a dedicated database with the same local-transaction rules, and let merchant-wide totals become a sum over databases. Finally, rate-limit per merchant so one burst cannot take the shared workers.

Reconciliation. A daily job compares the provider's settlement report with our ledger, matching on the provider reference. It lists four kinds of difference: only in our ledger, only in their report, an amount mismatch, and a state mismatch. Each is fixed by an explicit compensating entry or by resolving a stuck attempt or movement, with no row edited. Reconciliation is the backstop for what every earlier safeguard missed, so it runs even when nothing looks wrong.
deep-dives.ask: Let's go deeper on the parts that worry you most. What happens when the provider charges the card and your process dies right after?
deep-dives.say: For the crash, my first attempt is to call the provider and then write the result, which double charges if we die in between. So I write an attempt row, or a money-movement row for a capture, with our own reference before calling the provider and pass that reference along. A recovery worker looks up stuck attempts and movements by reference, and if the lookup finds nothing it repeats the call with the same reference. On the other three worries: for webhooks, I store each event under its unique id, reply fast, and run it through the state machine. For timeouts, I treat the outcome as unknown, retry within a budget, then ask the provider. For consistency, payment and ledger commit in one local transaction, with an outbox for everything outside.
deep-dives.tip: For each weak spot give a first attempt, say how it breaks, then the better design and its cost. A cost named without prompting reads as judgement.

That merchant sees slowness or limit errors
Per-merchant limits, a dedicated database for the largest merchants, and a separate worker pool.

blocks.text: The one rule behind the table: when the store is unsure, it says pending and keeps the evidence, and a worker resolves it later. It never guesses a final answer to look responsive.
Adyen's idempotency page covers what a client may do when Adyen's own idempotency store is unavailable, and this design pauses the charge path and asks merchants to retry later.
Amazon's post on timeouts and retries also discusses the cost of circuit breakers, the source of the caution in the Down row of this table.
Amazon's write-sharding page and Google's Spanner schema guide both treat hot keys in partitioned stores, and Google describes the trouble as "too many requests are sent to the same server".

Stripe's payout report and Adyen's settlement details report show how a provider lets a merchant match its money records, and Adyen states the purpose as "Use report to reconcile your settlements on a transaction level."

PostgreSQL's warm standby documentation describes the loss window of an asynchronous standby, and its synchronous replication section describes the wait-for-confirmation mode this store would need; it states the window as "there is a window for data loss should the primary server suffer a catastrophic failure".

failure-modes.ask: Go through the parts. What can fail, what does the merchant see, and how does the system recover?
failure-modes.say: I go component by component. If the API crashes anywhere around the provider call, the merchant sees a connection error, then a conflict status that tells it to retry later, then pending, while the recovery worker resolves the attempt or movement by lookup or by repeating the call with the same reference. If the provider is slow or down, we retry within a budget and a breaker stops new calls. If the store fails over, we only promote a replica that holds every committed attempt, movement and key row. Duplicate events are dropped by their ids, and a mismatch is found by reconciliation and fixed with a compensating entry that a reviewer approves, or by resolving the stuck attempt or movement.
failure-modes.tip: Walk the parts in the order a request meets them, and for each give what the user sees. Name the safe default, here pending, so recovery has something to start from.

blocks.text: Four textbook answers that sound right in an interview and are wrong or too costly here.

Two-phase commit across the payment and the ledger. The textbook says atomic commit across services keeps them consistent. Here it ties the charge path to a coordinator, and the one participant that matters most, the card network, cannot join. Say instead: keep what we own in one local transaction, and make the outside calls safe to repeat.
An authorization with a later void is itself a tentative operation: a promise that can still be cancelled. That is the shape that replaces atomic commit across parties we do not control.

Helland's 2007 paper argues for building large systems without distributed transactions: "In general, application developers simply do not implement large scalable applications assuming distributed transactions."

Exactly-once delivery from a queue. The textbook says to buy a broker with that property. Inside one system that controls both the log and the effect it can be real, and a broker can remove duplicates caused by producer resends. A charge is an effect on an outside provider that has to cooperate, so for us the dependable form is at-least-once delivery, a repeat-safe charge call keyed by our reference, and idempotent receivers. Between the payment and the ledger the question disappears, because both live in one database.

The Kafka design page, the SQS and RabbitMQ documentation and Google's Pub/Sub page all deal with duplicate delivery and where exactly-once stops; Kafka says: "Exactly-once delivery for other destination systems generally requires cooperation with such systems".

One big database transaction around the whole payment. The textbook says wrap the provider call and the writes in a transaction so they cannot disagree. Holding locks while waiting on a slow outside party blocks other work, and the provider's side cannot be rolled back by us in any case. Say instead: two short transactions with the attempt row between them, and the provider reference as the thread that ties them.

Sagas for everything. A saga strings together local steps, each committing on its own, and pays back completed steps with compensations. It fits the steps between our own stores. A captured charge is already in the customer's bank world, so a compensation here is a new record: a void before capture, a refund after. The ledger shows both the charge and the reversal.

The 1987 sagas paper and Hohpe's 2004 essay both describe compensating steps, and Hohpe lists as the last option to "undo operations that were already completed to put the system back into a consistent state".

against-the-grain.ask: A textbook would reach for two-phase commit here. Would you?
against-the-grain.say: I would not, and I would avoid exactly-once delivery too. Two-phase commit would tie the charge path to a coordinator, and the card network cannot take part anyway, so I keep what we own in one local transaction and make outside calls safe to repeat. Exactly-once is real only where one system controls both the log and the effect, so a broker's own mode is fine inside the broker and stops at the provider call. A charge is an effect at the provider, so I use at-least-once delivery, a repeat-safe call keyed by our reference, and idempotent receivers. I also would not hold a database transaction open across the provider call.
against-the-grain.tip: When you reject a textbook answer, name the assumption it needs and show that it fails here. Then say what you use instead and what that costs.

strong-answer.talkTrack: A payment gateway sits between merchants and outside providers that I cannot roll back. So I rank correctness first: never charge twice, always record what moved. I scope to create, authorize, capture and void, and I leave vaults, fraud and payouts out. The core is a payment state machine with final states, an attempt or money-movement record written before every provider call, and an idempotency key stored in the same transaction as the payment. Money goes into an append-only, double-entry ledger in the same local transaction as the state change, so I need no distributed transaction. Provider events and merchant events both go through tables, an inbox and an outbox, because delivery is at least once and I make every step safe to repeat. A timeout means unknown, so I retry within a budget or ask the provider by reference, and I answer pending when I cannot be sure. A reconciler compares the provider's reports with my ledger. I scale by merchant partition and watch for hot merchants.

levels.mid: My first pass covers the shape: clear scope, the calls, a payment record with states, a provider adapter, an idempotency key so a retry does not charge twice, and a webhook for the result. I can say why capture comes after authorization and what a ledger is for, and I can explain each box and what happens on a simple failure.
levels.senior: My deeper pass takes the weak spots unprompted. I separate attempts from payments, say that a timeout leaves the outcome unknown and the payment unchanged, and choose between retrying and asking with a stated reason. I handle duplicate and reordered events with a unique event id and a state machine, keep the ledger in the same transaction as the state, and state the cost of each choice, such as the extra write before every provider call and the pending answer merchants must handle.
levels.staff: My judgement pass argues where the usual answer is wrong: why two-phase commit, and exactly-once delivery across the provider call, are the wrong tools, and what takes their place. I set out how each component fails and the order of recovery, name what reconciliation catches that nothing else does, and plan for hot merchants, retention and the growth of history. I name the first metric to watch, the count and age of attempts and movements stuck in sent, and say what I would change if a provider offered no safe repeat or lookup.

followUps.ask: A merchant sends the same idempotency key with a different amount. What happens?
followUps.answer: The server compares the request to the fingerprint saved with the key and sees a mismatch. It refuses with an unprocessable-content status and does nothing else. The client reused a key for a different operation, which is a bug on their side, and silently replaying the old reply would hide it.

followUps.ask: How long do you keep idempotency records, and what protects a payment after they expire?
followUps.answer: Longer than the longest time a merchant's client retries, plus margin; I would state a number for the exercise and ask the merchants. After expiry, the unique merchant order reference refuses a second payment for the same order unless the first one failed, was voided or expired. Keys protect against retries of one call. The order reference protects against a repeated intent.

followUps.ask: The provider is down. Do you send traffic to another one?
followUps.answer: For new payments, yes, once a breaker opens and the second provider is ready. For a payment whose attempt is unknown, no. Moving it before the first provider answers risks two charges. Resolve the unknown attempt first, by lookup or by repeating the call with the same reference, then decide.

followUps.ask: How do you reconcile, and what happens on a mismatch?
followUps.answer: A scheduled job matches the provider's settlement report against our ledger by provider reference and lists differences in four kinds. Each is fixed with an explicit compensating entry or by resolving a stuck attempt or movement, with a person approving. We never edit a row. Reports are the final safety net, so the job runs even when everything looks fine.

followUps.ask: How would you add refunds, and partial capture later?
followUps.answer: Full capture is the scope here. A refund is a new money movement that points at the payment and posts reversing ledger entries in its own balanced transaction, with its own idempotency key. If partial capture were added later, each capture would be its own movement with its own id and entries. The payment's final state stays final, and the detail lives in the movement rows.

followUps.ask: One merchant is a large share of all traffic. What changes?
followUps.answer: Contention comes first from single rows, so balances become sums of entries with checkpoints and no row is updated per payment, and the key insert and the payment row, whose order reference is unique, stay in one local transaction. Then per-merchant limits and a separate worker pool. Sub-partitions inside one database relieve hot rows only. If the merchant saturates the primary, it gets a dedicated database with the same rules, and merchant totals become sums over databases.

followUps.ask: How does a merchant verify that an event really came from you?
followUps.answer: We sign the raw body with a secret shared with that merchant and include a signed timestamp. The merchant recomputes the signature on the raw bytes, rejects old timestamps to stop replay, and ignores event ids it has already handled. When the secret changes, retries of older events are signed with the old secret, so the receiver accepts both for a short period.

followUps.ask: Why not use a queue with exactly-once delivery between the payment and ledger services?
followUps.answer: Exactly-once holds where one system controls both the log and the effect, so a broker's own mode is fine inside the broker and stops at the provider call. Between the payment and the ledger we avoid the question by using one database. For the charge itself the effect lives at the provider, who has to cooperate, so we make the call repeat-safe by reference and keep delivery at least once.

followUps.ask: How would you move a merchant to another partition?
followUps.answer: Copy the merchant's rows to the target while the source keeps serving, and keep the copy fed from the change log. Then pause that merchant's writes briefly, check that row counts and ledger sums match, and switch the routing entry. Because the partition key is the merchant, the payment, its attempts, movements, entries, key records and outbox rows travel together, so a capture is one local transaction before and after. In-progress rows move too, so a retry during the move still finds its key. The costs are a short write pause for that merchant and a routing directory that becomes a dependency of every request.

followUps.ask: What changes with more than one region, and what recovery targets do you set?
followUps.answer: I would state two targets first: how much committed data we may lose, and how long the charge path may be down. For money the first is nothing, which needs synchronous replication of the payment store to a second site, paid for in write latency on every attempt. A warm standby region with its own workers takes over, and recovery and reconciliation cover payments where the provider had already acted. Writing in two regions for one merchant needs a single owner region per merchant, because two owners could both move the same payment. This page assumes one region, so this is the first thing I would add.

followUps.ask: Some payment methods settle later or need the customer to act. How does that fit?
followUps.answer: They break the authorize-then-capture shape. A bank transfer or wallet has a customer step and a result that arrives hours or days later, and some methods ask the customer to authenticate in their own app before the provider approves. I would add a state before authorized, such as awaiting customer action, with an expiry, and let only the provider's signed event or a lookup move it on. Idempotency, the inbox and reconciliation stay as they are. What changes is that pending can last long, so merchants rely on the event and need a clear expiry.

followUps.ask: What do you monitor, and what pages the on-call?
followUps.answer: Start with the stuck metric: count and age of attempts and movements in sent. Add the age of the oldest unprocessed inbound event and undelivered outbound event, any ledger transaction that does not balance, reconciliation differences by kind, the provider's error and timeout rate, and the share of pending replies. Page for symptoms a user feels: stuck age past its deadline, errors on the charge path, an unbalanced ledger. Everything else goes on dashboards. An objective for the charge path and a budget for it decide when to stop shipping changes.

followUps.ask: Which database would you pick, and what does isolation change?
followUps.answer: A relational store with transactions inside a partition, because a capture needs the state change, balanced entries and the outbox row to commit together, and because unique constraints do real work here: the key per merchant, the order reference, the provider event id and the ledger transaction id. A unique constraint is enforced by its index at any isolation level. Weaker isolation allows read-then-write races, so state changes use a version check. A distributed store also works if it gives transactions within one merchant's partition and enforces uniqueness there; if uniqueness holds only per node, the key and order-reference protections weaken.

followUps.ask: How do you handle several currencies and conversion?
followUps.answer: Every amount is a whole number of the smallest unit with its currency code, and amounts of different currencies are never added. A conversion is its own money movement that records the rate, both amounts and the rounding rule. It posts entries that balance within each currency, using a conversion account on each side. The rate is recorded with the payment so a later dispute can replay it. Rounding happens in one place, and any leftover smallest unit is an explicit entry instead of a silent loss.

followUps.ask: Do merchants get events in order, and how long do you retry?
followUps.answer: We do not promise global order. Each event carries the payment id, the new state and a version or created time, so a receiver can ignore an older one, and the safe habit is to treat an event as a hint and call Get payment. Ordering within one payment is possible by sending its events one at a time, but one slow endpoint then blocks that merchant's stream. Delivery is at least once, so events repeat. The retry window is a choice; I would set it with merchants to be longer than their usual outage, and afterwards they rely on Get payment and a replay list in the dashboard.

followUps.ask: How do you test the failure paths?
followUps.answer: The provider sits behind the adapter, so tests swap in a fake that can time out after it has charged, answer twice, reorder or drop events and send a late authorization. For the crash dive I stop the process between each pair of writes and the provider call, restart it, and check the invariants: one charge per payment, a balanced ledger, nothing left in sent. The provider's sandbox serves contract checks, not failure injection, since it will not lose a reply on request. In production, a small rate of injected faults on the adapter shows that recovery still works.

strong-answer.ask: Pull it together for me in about a minute, then tell me what you would do with more time.
strong-answer.say: A gateway sits between merchants and outside providers I cannot roll back, so correctness of money ranks first: never charge twice, always record what moved. Scope is create, authorize, capture and void. The core is a payment state machine with final states, an attempt or money-movement row written before every provider call, and an idempotency key stored in the same transaction as the payment. Money goes into an append-only, double-entry ledger in the same local transaction as the state change. A timeout means unknown, so I retry within a budget or ask the provider, and answer pending meanwhile. A reconciler compares the provider's reports with my ledger. With more time I would load test one partition and add a second provider.
strong-answer.tip: Practise a short version out loud, then the long one. Leave a minute at the end to say what you would do next and what you would measure.

items.mistake: Treating a timeout as a failure and telling the merchant to retry with a new request.
items.fix: A timeout is unknown. Keep the attempt and the provider reference, retry the same request within a budget, or ask the provider, and answer pending meanwhile.

items.mistake: Putting the idempotency key in a cache or a separate store from the payment.
items.fix: Write the key and the payment in one transaction. Two stores can disagree after a crash, and then the key protects nothing.

items.mistake: Updating a balance field on each payment, or editing a ledger row to fix a mistake.
items.fix: Append entries only, fix errors with a reversing entry, and compute balances from entries and checkpoints. This keeps the history auditable and avoids a hot row.

items.mistake: Wrapping the provider call and the database writes in one transaction, or reaching for two-phase commit.
items.fix: Use short local transactions around a durable attempt or money-movement row, make outside calls safe to repeat, and use an outbox for anything that must follow a commit.

items.mistake: Trusting webhook order and uniqueness, or doing the work before replying.
items.fix: Store the event under its unique id, reply fast, process later, and apply it only if the state machine allows the move. Ask the provider when the order is unclear.

items.mistake: Skipping reconciliation because every step is idempotent.
items.fix: Idempotency prevents duplicates it knows about. Only comparison with the provider's reports finds what slipped through, such as a charge no event ever described.

items.mistake: Opening with the diagram and ignoring scope, so the design never meets a real requirement.
items.fix: Spend the first minutes on scope and ranked qualities. Put numbers in only where they change a choice.

mistakes.ask: What would you warn a new engineer about when they build this?
mistakes.say: Treating a timeout as a failure is the first warning, because the card may already be charged. Then keeping the idempotency key away from the payment's transaction, editing ledger rows or updating balances in place, wrapping the provider call in a database transaction, trusting webhook order, skipping reconciliation, and opening with the diagram instead of the scope. The habit that avoids most of these is to write the intent first, append to the ledger and leave history untouched, and treat each event as a claim to check.
mistakes.tip: Pair every warning with its fix in one line, and rank the warnings by how much damage each does. A short ranked list is easier to remember than a long flat one.

curiosities.text: More than a trillion ledger entries had to move to a new store over two years, with no downtime and no outage. How do you prove a copy that large is right?

The largest offline validation job in one ledger move compared 760 billion records, 70 TB compressed. The post says live shadow validation cannot give strong guarantees for rarely accessed history. Why was that gap there?
In one large ledger, card holds must be visible to the next read, while payment history may lag a few seconds. Why would one ledger want both rules?
One backfill example: 100 billion records at 10,000 a second take 120 days, while production normally handles 1,000 a second. The post says to scale the job up in small steps. Why small?
In a stack five deep with three retries at each layer, a failing database would see 243x the load. Where do the retries belong?
A retry budget lets a client retry only while retries are below 10% of its requests, and layering it brings growth to 1.1x in the general case. Why such a small budget?
One paper's transaction layer, in its worst case of writing a single cell and committing, costs roughly four times the raw store, and the team accepted that overhead. What did it buy?

blocks.text: Pacing advice (not any company's process): spend the opening on scope, put a first design on the board early, use most of the time on the parts that carry the risk, and keep a few minutes at the end for failures and next steps.

items: Clarify before you draw. Spend the opening on questions about who uses the system, how big it gets and what must never happen.
State assumptions aloud as you make them. The interviewer can correct one early, and a wrong guess left unspoken costs the whole design.
Agree priorities. Name the two or three qualities that matter most for this system, so every later trade-off has a stated reason.
Draw early and keep to it. Put a rough picture up soon, update it as the design changes, and point at it when you talk.
Think aloud. A silent minute hides your reasoning, and the interviewer can only help with what they can hear.
Name the trade-off and its cost with every choice. Say what you gain, what you pay, and what would make the other choice better.
Check in at the end of each part. A short question, such as whether to go deeper here or move on, keeps you on what matters to them.

blocks.text: Be ready for a follow-up that changes a constraint, for example a much larger scale, a dependency that disappears, or a new requirement. When it happens, restate the new constraint, say which parts of the design it touches and which stay as they are, and change only those.
When you are stuck, say so and say what you do know. Name the hard part, pick the simplest option that could work, give its weakness, and carry on. Return to the hard part with whatever time is left.
Meta's careers blog (October 2022) advises on how to open a design round: "Make it a conversation: Be sure to ask clarifying questions. But make sure you drive towards a good solution."
Microsoft's interview tips (no date shown) say how to start answering an interview question: "start by asking clarifying questions and stating your assumptions."

Atlassian's backend interview guide (no date shown; the PDF's file metadata is from 2023, about three years old) addresses communicating while you work: "continue to communicate with your interviewer as you progress towards a solution."

Amazon's SDE II preparation page (no date shown) supports asking questions as the design takes shape: "Your interviewer will ask questions related to your design, and you should ask questions to complete and validate your design."

Flipkart's guide for software engineers (the PDF shows no date; its file metadata is from 2020, about six years old) advises making your thinking visible: "You can help the interviewers understand your thought process by thinking out loud."
